metaTitle: Hiring a Retaining Wall Contractor in Ontario
metaDescription: Segmental block vs stone vs poured concrete, drainage, the 1 metre permit rule, and how to vet an Ontario retaining wall contractor before you sign.
h1: How to Hire a Retaining Wall Contractor in Ontario
summary: Materials, drainage, the 1 metre engineering rule, and what separates a real retaining wall contractor from a landscaper with a truck.
intro: A retaining wall looks simple from the sidewalk, a row of stacked material holding back a slope, but it is doing real structural work against soil pressure, frost, and water year after year. Ontario's freeze thaw cycles are unforgiving on walls built without proper drainage or footings, and a wall that fails can take a chunk of your yard or a fence with it. This guide covers material choices, why drainage matters more than the facing, when engineered drawings are required, and how to spot a contractor who actually specializes in retaining walls.

sections.heading: Segmental block, natural stone, or poured concrete

blocks.text: Most residential retaining walls in Ontario use one of three systems. Segmental retaining wall block, often called SRW block, is the most common choice under about a metre. The units have a built in setback and interlocking lip, so a trained installer can build a wall that leans slightly into the slope without mortar. It installs quickly, comes in many colours and textures, and is usually the most budget friendly option per square foot.

Natural stone walls, whether dry stacked fieldstone or mortared armour stone, cost more per square foot because the material is heavier and slower to place. Armour stone is popular in southwestern Ontario because large boulders serve as both structure and finished look with little facing needed. Dry stacked stone relies entirely on the weight and friction of the stones, so the installer's skill in placing each piece matters enormously.

Poured concrete walls, reinforced with rebar and formed on site, are typically reserved for taller walls, walls carrying a driveway or structural load, or a thin profile against a property line. They cost more upfront because of formwork and curing time, but carry loads that block or dry stacked stone cannot, and are the usual choice once an engineer is involved.

items: Segmental block: budget friendly, fast install, good for walls under about a metre
Natural stone (armour stone or dry stack): higher material cost, relies heavily on installer skill
Poured concrete: highest upfront cost, needed for tall walls or structural loads, usually engineer designed

sections.heading: Why drainage matters more than the facing material

blocks.text: Almost every retaining wall failure a homeowner sees, bulging, leaning, or a toppled section, traces back to water, not the facing material. Saturated soil becomes dramatically heavier, and in an Ontario winter it freezes and expands, pushing outward with far more force than dry soil ever would. A wall that looks identical from the front can be built two completely different ways behind the scenes, and only time will tell you which one you got.

A properly built wall includes a compacted granular base below frost depth, clean crushed stone behind the wall face, a perforated drainage pipe, often called a weeping tile, to carry water away, and geotextile fabric to keep soil particles from clogging the stone over time. Backfill should be a free draining granular material, not the clay heavy native soil dug out of the hole, since clay holds water against the wall instead of letting it pass through.
If a quote does not mention drainage stone, a weeping tile, or a compacted base, ask how water behind the wall will be managed. A vague answer is a serious warning sign.

Backfill compaction matters just as much. It needs to be placed and compacted in thin lifts, not dumped in all at once, or the soil will settle unevenly and pull the wall out of alignment. Ask how the contractor compacts backfill and in what lift thickness, a specific answer is a good sign of real experience.

sections.heading: The Ontario 1 metre rule: permits and engineering

blocks.text: In most Ontario municipalities, a retaining wall taller than roughly 1 metre, about 3.3 feet, measured footing to top, triggers a building permit requirement and often needs engineered drawings stamped by a professional engineer. This exists because taller walls hold back significantly more soil pressure, and a failure at that height poses a real safety risk to whatever sits above or below it.

The exact height and documentation required varies by municipality, so treat this as a starting point, not gospel. Some municipalities measure differently or add rules for walls near a property line or supporting a surcharge load such as a driveway or pool. Check with your local building department before work starts, not after.

items.title: Confirm wall height and surcharge loads
items.text: Measure footing to top, and note anything the wall will support above it, such as a driveway or pool deck, since that adds load beyond the soil itself.

items.title: Call your municipal building department
items.text: Ask whether a permit is required at your wall's height and what documents, such as engineered drawings, the department expects.

items.title: Get engineered drawings if required
items.text: For taller walls, an engineer designs the wall system, footing depth, drainage, and reinforcement for your soil conditions.

items.title: Keep permit and inspection records
items.text: A closed permit with inspection sign off protects you at resale or if a future problem raises questions about the build.

sections.heading: Why engineering matters for taller walls

blocks.text: It is tempting to see the requirement as red tape, but the physics are real. Soil pressure against a retaining structure increases with the square of the wall height, so a wall twice as tall holds back far more than twice the pressure. Generic manufacturer guidelines cover standard installation, but past roughly a metre they are no longer a safe substitute for a design accounting for your soil type, slope, drainage, and any load above the wall.

An engineer will typically specify footing depth and width, whether the wall needs geogrid reinforcement, backfill and compaction requirements, and site specific drainage, and may recommend a soil test since clay heavy or disturbed fill behaves differently than stable native soil. Skipping engineering on a wall that needs it is a costly mistake, since a failed tall wall often takes fencing, patios, or landscaping down with it. The engineering fee is cheap insurance against that outcome.

sections.heading: Choosing a contractor with retaining wall specific experience

blocks.text: Retaining walls sit between landscaping and structural construction, and many general landscaping companies will quote a wall project without deep experience in the drainage and grading details that determine whether it lasts. A contractor with a real portfolio of completed walls similar in height and material to yours is a safer bet than a lawn and garden company that added walls to its service list.

Ask to see photos of walls that have been in the ground for a few years, not just freshly finished projects, since drainage and compaction problems often take one or two freeze thaw cycles to show themselves. A contractor confident in their work will have no problem showing older projects and, ideally, connecting you with a past client.

items: Ask for photos or addresses of walls built at least two winters ago, not just recent work
Ask specifically how they handle drainage stone, weeping tile, and backfill compaction
Confirm they carry general liability insurance and, if trades are involved, current WSIB clearance
For any wall approaching the 1 metre threshold, confirm they will pull the permit and work from engineered drawings rather than eyeballing it
Get a written scope that specifies wall height, material, drainage details, and base depth, not just a lump sum price

blocks.text: Our directory at /winners can help narrow the field to businesses recognized for consistent workmanship. Whatever contractor you choose, a clear written scope and at least three quotes from businesses with a real retaining wall portfolio will put you in a stronger position than picking on price alone.

checklist: Measure your wall height from footing to top, including any slope, to know if you are near the 1 metre permit threshold
Call your municipal building department before design work starts to confirm permit and engineering requirements
Choose a material, segmental block, natural stone, or poured concrete, based on height, budget, and desired look
Confirm the quote includes a compacted base, drainage stone, weeping tile, and geotextile fabric, not just the visible facing
Ask how backfill will be compacted and in what lift thickness
For taller walls, get engineered drawings from a licensed engineer before construction begins
Ask to see photos of the contractor's walls that have been in the ground for at least two winters
Confirm liability insurance and, if applicable, WSIB clearance for any subcontracted trades
Get a written scope specifying wall height, material, drainage system, and base depth
Keep permit and inspection paperwork on file in case of a future sale or dispute

faq.q: Do I really need a permit for a small retaining wall?
faq.a: It depends on height and your municipality. Many Ontario municipalities set the threshold around 1 metre from footing to top, but some measure differently or apply lower thresholds near property lines, so check with your local building department before assuming a small wall is exempt.

faq.q: Can I build a retaining wall myself without a contractor?
faq.a: For a low wall, under about half a metre, with good drainage, some homeowners do it themselves successfully. Anything approaching the permit threshold, or any wall supporting a driveway, deck, or slope near a structure, is worth hiring a specialist for given the consequences of a failure.

faq.q: How long should a properly built retaining wall last?
faq.a: A wall built with proper drainage, base depth, and compaction can last decades with minimal maintenance. Most failures within the first few years trace back to skipped drainage or inadequate backfill compaction rather than the facing material itself.

faq.q: Is natural stone always better than segmental block?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Natural stone often costs more and depends heavily on the installer's skill in placing individual stones, while a well engineered segmental block wall from a reputable manufacturer can be just as durable and considerably more budget friendly for many yards.
